questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The distance $d$, in meters, that a car has traveled after $t$ seconds can be modeled by the function $d(t)=\frac{2{t}^{3}+7t}{t+1}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the distance traveled when $t=2$ seconds?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the distance traveled when $t=2$ seconds is equal to ${d}^{′}(2).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{d}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{t}^{3}+7t}{t+1}) \\  & =\frac{(6{t}^{2}+7)(t+1)-(2{t}^{3}+7t)(1)}{(t+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{t}^{3}+6{t}^{2}+7}{(t+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{d}^{′}(2) & =\frac{4(2)^{3}+6(2)^{2}+7}{((2)+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{32+24+7}{9} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the distance traveled when $t=2$ seconds is $7$ meters per second.

The surface area $A$ of the sphere above is increasing. The radius of the sphere is $r.$ Find the rate of change of the surface area of a sphere with respect to its radius.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the surface area of the sphere is given by  

$$
A=A(r)=4\pi {r}^{2}
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(r)$ with respect to its radius $r$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi (2r) \\  & =8\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
In an acoustics lab, the ambient noise power (in decibels) at frequency $f$ (in $\text{kHz}$) is modeled by the function

$$
N(f)={2}^{-2{f}^{2}}.
$$

What is the exact value of the instantaneous rate at which the noise power is changing with respect to frequency when $f=2\,\text{kHz}?$ 

The instantaneous rate of change when $f=2\,\text{kHz}$ is 
{{field-1}} decibels per $\text{kHz}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change at which the ambient noise power is changing when $f=2$ kHz is equal to ${N}^{′}(2).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $N(f)$ with respect to $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{N}^{′}(f) & =\frac{d}{df}({2}^{-2{f}^{2}}) \\  & ={2}^{-2{f}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\cdot (-4f) \\  & =-4f\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,{2}^{-2{f}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $f=2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{N}^{′}(2) & =-4(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,{2}^{-2(2)^{2}} \\  & =-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,{2}^{-8} \\  & =-\frac{8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{256} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the ambient noise power is changing when $f=2\,\text{kHz}$ is $-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{32}$ decibels per $\text{kHz}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
questions.problem:
The volume of a right square pyramid is increasing. Given that its height $h$ is always twice the length of a base, find the rate of change of the volume of the pyramid with respect to its base length $s.$

*Hint*: The volume of a right square pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{s}^{2}h.$ 

The rate of change of the pyramid’s volume with respect to $s$ is 
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that $h=2s,$ so we can express the volume of the pyramid $V$ as a function of the base edge length $s$ by substituting $h=2s$ in the formula of the volume. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V(s) & =\frac{1}{3}{s}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{s}^{2}(2s) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $V(s)$ with respect to $s$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(s) & =\frac{d}{ds}\,(\frac{2}{3}{s}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{d}{ds}\,({s}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{s}^{2} \\  & =2{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the rate of change of the pyramid’s volume with respect to its base length $s$ is $2{s}^{2}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14004055/assets/34966965452968c2f186efcfbec70591eded02e926eaaac8b90409381b2c8da8.png)

The area of an equilateral triangle is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the area of the equilateral triangle is increasing with respect to its side length at the moment when its side length is equal to $s=4\,\text{in}.$  

*Hint*: The area of an equilateral triangle is $A=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}{s}^{2}.$ 

The instantaneous rate of change at the moment when its side length is $4$ inches is equal to
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{in}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the area of the equilateral triangle with side $s$ is given by  

$$
A=A(s)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}{s}^{2}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $A(s)$  with respect to $s$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}{s}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\cdot (2s) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $s=4$ gives

$$
{A}^{′}(4)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 4=2\sqrt{3}.
$$

 

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at the moment when the length of the side is $s=4\,\text{in}$ is $2\sqrt{3}\,{\text{in}}^{2}/\text{in}.$
